chapter: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
title: Lena Horne's kindness and the dressing room
summary: Lena Horne let Nellie sit in her dressing room during intermissions and always brought her refreshments, insisting on first names.

bands.name: Dootsie Williams and the Chocolate Drops

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: That's right. See Lena was the -- they brought her out here. This was before she got into the movies, you see. And the one thing I must say about her, she is -- was and still is a marvelous person as well as a tremendous performer, you know. I just -- since that time I have really come in contact, because of my position -- I have had the pleasure of meeting many people, names, big names in the business, stars so to speak, but Lena Horne was always so very warm and cordial and so very kind, you know, and this left a great impression on me. I just love Lena today for that, because at that time I wasn't known. You know, I was just a little piano player with a little group, you know.
But the fellow who owned the club at that time, Felix Young, asked Lena could -- he says -- well, like most clubs they have a room for the band boys, you know,

and of course everybody during intermission time, when they'd take their intermission, we all sat in the band room. Well, you know how the musicians are, the guys are talking and cracking and making jokes and whatever. So Felix said -- he says, "Listen, I'm going to ask Miss Horne if it'll be all right for you to sit in her dressing room. Would it be all right with you if I asked her?" And I said, "Well, I don't want to impose on her. I don't want to bother her, because she needs her privacy." He said, "No, she's not like that. Let me ask her." And he went and asked Lena Horne. He says, "Miss Horne," he says, "would you mind if the piano player, the girl with the group, would you mind if she sat in her, you know, if she didn't bother you?" She said, "By all means let her sit in here." And he said, "Well, there's no place for her. She's in there with the band." But I was the only girl, you know. I don't know how many guys were in the band. I guess about eight or ten guys, no doubt, and then there were four people -- three people including myself, in our group, you know. So he said all right. So he came back out and told me, "Miss Horne said she'd be grateful --," not grateful, I don't mean that, but she'd be very happy to have you sit in there. You're most welcome. And so I went on in, you know, but I didn't ever bother her. I'd bring a book or something with me to read, you know. And she was just as kind to me, and she said -- every time she'd get coffee or get a drink or get

something for herself, she'd say, "Bring something for Nellie. Bring something for Nellie." And I would say, "Oh, no, Miss Horne." And she'd say, "Don't call me Miss Horne. Call me Lena. Just call me Lena." But you know, I was just used to that, giving her the respect. But I just loved her. But unfortunately I took sick while I was on that job. I had a terrible problem with a tooth, and this tooth had bothered me for, oh, I bet two or three years prior to this, and my dentist told me it was a dangerous tooth. It was aching me at the time, you know, and now when I went to him my husband and I were together, and he said, "Now, I'm going to pack this tooth for you." He says, "I can't extract it, but I'm going to pack it for you. This tooth is infected. You're going to have to have this tooth taken out. But in about two or three weeks I want you to come back and I'm going to extract it." But he says, "I'll pack it temporarily for you now." He packed it and it stopped hurting and I didn't think about it. I forgot the tooth was in my head. I forgot it was there. I didn't even think about it another time. Didn't hurt me one bit.
